title: Sections have their own vocabulary: which word is written depends on the section
statement: In paragraph text, the mutual information between a certain word and the illustration section of its page is greater than when the words are dealt out at random across pages.
source: Registers the section vocabularies (Currier 1976; Layfield and Davis 2026, K-003) with the context_mi statistic, as a long-range target for generators next to F-009 (page) and F-011 (neighbouring pages). Public practice split (Zandbergen-Landini): 1.183 bits on the evaluation pages and 0.814 on the training pages, both p = 0.005 against 199 shuffles; Takahashi 1.207 and RF 1.220 on the evaluation pages, both passing. The plug-in value is biased upward and grows as the sample shrinks, so no level is registered, only the comparison with the shuffle. What it does and does not add. The null deals words across all pages, so it also destroys page-level vocabulary: a text whose pages differ but whose sections do not would pass as well, and this fact is therefore not independent of F-009 and F-011. A null that keeps pages whole and moves them between sections would isolate the section; the measurement language has none (shuffling words within a section leaves the statistic unchanged by construction, p = 0.96). Not evidence of language: any book whose parts treat different matter passes. As a generator target, on the practice split: a line-restarting glyph chain with one table gives 0.95 and fails (two seeds); the same chain with a table that drifts through the public pages at the pace of the book and reuse of recent and familiar words gives 1.11 to 1.13 and passes (three runs). So it separates one-table procedures from those whose tables change along the book, as F-011 does, and is not expected to resist the procedure already on the record.
